phonemes.desc: Voiced velar stop [ɡ], as in English 'give', and short front [e], as in 'bed'; the stressed first syllable, as in all Old Norse words.
The labiodental fricative, voiced toward [v] between the vowel and the glide — Old Norse f softens in voiced company, as in gefa itself.
Palatal glide [j], short close back [u], and dental [n]; the manuscripts write this ending -jun, never -jon.

pronunciation.approximation: 'GEV-yoon' — the g hard as in 'give', the e short as in 'bed', the second syllable like 'yoon' with a light v-glide before it; stress the first syllable, as in modern Icelandic Gefjun.

kin.form: Gefjun, the ploughing goddess; from gefa, 'to give'.

kin.label: The root verb
kin.form: gefa, 'to give' — the same word as English give and German geben.

kin.label: Freyja's byname
kin.form: Gefn, 'the giver' — the name's closest divine relative, from the same root.

kin.label: Modern Icelandic
kin.form: Gefjun, unchanged; older English books write the Latinized Gefion.

pronunciation.note: Old Norse Gefjun derives transparently from gefa, 'to give': Cleasby-Vigfusson enter the goddess under that root, and Zoëga glosses the name as the giver. The restoration Gefjun is plain ASCII — the normalized Old Norse spelling carries no diacritic and no distinctive letter — so the mechanical rule places the name in Tier 2. The working ASCII form 'gefjon' respells the ending with an o; the manuscripts know only Gefjun.

domains.title: The Ploughing Goddess
domains.subtitle: The Four Oxen, the Wager of King Gylfi, and the Making of Zealand
domains.lead: Gefjun is the giver who made an island: the Æsir-born goddess who accepted King Gylfi's jest of a plough-land — as much as four oxen could turn in a day and a night — and answered it by begetting four sons on a giant, yoking them as oxen, and dragging the whole of Zealand out of Sweden into the sea.

cards.name: The Four Oxen
cards.desc: Her sons by a giant of Jötunheimr, shape-changed into draught-beasts — Bragi counts them: eight eyes and four heads.

cards.name: The Plough
cards.desc: Driven so deep and hard that it tore the bedrock: the instrument by which a piece of Sweden became an island.

cards.name: Zealand (Selund)
cards.desc: The land she set in the sound and named — drawn west, Ynglinga saga says, until it lay opposite Odense.

cards.name: Lake Mälaren
cards.desc: The mould the island was cast from: water filled the wound, and the lake's bays answer Zealand's headlands.

symbols.name: The plough
symbols.meaning: Creation by furrow: land made by turning earth — the oldest technology of order doing the work of a god

symbols.name: The four oxen
symbols.meaning: Giant strength yoked to a goddess's purpose: brute force given direction

symbols.name: The plough-land
symbols.meaning: The wager's unit — a day and a night's ploughing, stretched within its own terms until it holds an island

symbols.name: The answering coasts
symbols.meaning: Zealand's headlands and Mälaren's bays: the two halves of one tear, the myth's own map

mythology.lead: Gefjun has one of the few land-creation myths in the whole Norse corpus, and it opens the Prose Edda itself: the ploughing of Zealand. Around that single great deed the sources add a catalogue entry, a dynastic marriage, and one sharp exchange in verse.

myths.title: The Plough-Land of King Gylfi
myths.text: When Snorri opens Gylfaginning, before Gylfi ever reaches Ásgarðr, he tells how the king was first tricked out of a piece of his kingdom. Gylfi gave a wandering beggar-woman, as reward for the entertainment she gave him, one plough-land in his realm — as much as four oxen could plough up in a day and a night. But the woman was of the family of the Æsir, and her name was Gefjun. She took four oxen out of Jötunheimr — her own sons, begotten on a certain giant — and set them before the plough. The share went so deep and hard that it tore the land loose, and the oxen drew it out into the sea and westward until it stopped in a sound. There Gefjun set the land and named it Selund, Zealand. And where the land had been taken from, the water filled in: that is now the lake called Lögrinn, Mälaren, and the bays of the lake, Snorri says, correspond to the headlands of Zealand.

myths.title: The Völva and the Founding of Lejre
myths.text: Heimskringla tells the same making as dynastic history. Gefjun, the saga says, was a spákona, a seeress, and Óðinn sent her north across the sound to look for land. King Gylfi met her and gave her one plough-land. She went to Jötunheimr, bore four sons to a giant there, changed them into the likeness of oxen, yoked them, and drew the land out into the sea westward, opposite Óðinsvé — Odense. Then the saga adds what the Edda leaves out: Gefjun settled on the land she had made and married Skjöldr, a son of Óðinn, and their seat was Hleiðra — Lejre, beside Roskilde, the royal seat of Denmark. The goddess who made the island also stood at the root of its kings: Skjöldr is the eponym of the Skjöldungar, the Scyldings whose line Beowulf opens by praising.

myths.title: Eight Eyes and Four Heads
myths.text: Both Snorri and the saga close the account with the same four lines, attributed to Bragi inn gamli Boddason, the ninth-century skald — the oldest datable witness to the story. In the verse's kennings, Gefjun gladly drew from Gylfi 'the wave-trove's free-hold' until smoke rose from the running sweat-beasts, and the oxen bore 'eight forehead-moons and four heads' as they carried off Denmark's increase. Eight eyes and four heads: the poet counts the team for us. The making of Zealand was already a fixed story, with fixed imagery, centuries before Snorri wrote it down.

myths.title: Fourth Among the Ásynjur
myths.text: In Gylfaginning's catalogue of the ásynjur, Gefjun stands fourth, after Frigg, Sága, and Eir, and Snorri gives her a single, startling office: 'she is a maiden, and those who die maidens serve her.' The sentence sits unresolved beside the Zealand story — the maiden of the catalogue is the giant's consort of the myth — and the tradition never reconciled the two. Skáldskaparmál keeps her in the þulur, the metrical name-lists of the ásynjur, where her name is licensed as a base-word in kennings for women: a skald praising a woman could reach for Gefjun as readily as for any goddess.

myths.title: The Necklace and the Fair Lad
myths.text: Gefjun speaks once in the Poetic Edda, and it costs her. In Lokasenna, as Loki works his way down the bench of goddesses at Ægir's feast, Gefjun intervenes: why, she asks, do you Æsir bandy bitter words here in the hall? Óðinn's rebuke is immediate — she is mad, he says, to rouse Loki, for Loki knows the fates of all as well as Óðinn himself. Then Loki turns on her with the only scandal the corpus attaches to her name: a fair youth once gave her a bright necklace, a sigli, and she wound her legs about him. The taunt echoes the necklace-stories of the other goddesses, and the poem moves on; nothing in the corpus answers it, and nothing repeats it.

lore.syncretism: Gefjun's nearest relative lives inside the pantheon itself. Gylfaginning names Gefn — 'the giver' — among Freyja's bynames, and both names stand on the same root, gefa; Simek treats the two as possibly once-connected figures, distinct in the surviving sources. Beyond the North, scholars have long set her story among the land-measure foundation legends of the ancient world — the type of tale in which a people explains how its territory was won by stretching a definition, Dido's ox-hide at Carthage being the classical case — with the difference that Gefjun stretches not a hide but a day's ploughing, and the unit she stretches is agricultural. Her other life is dynastic: through Skjöldr she belongs to the origin-complex of the Danish kings, the same stratum that produced Beowulf's Scyld Scefing and Saxo's Skioldus. The handbooks read the marriage as the point where myth and royal genealogy were deliberately joined — a plough-goddess at the root of a farming aristocracy's line.
lore.culturalLegacy: Gefjun's afterlife is monumental and national. The Gefion Fountain on Copenhagen's harbourfront — Anders Bundgaard's great bronze group, unveiled in 1908 as the Carlsberg Foundation's gift to the city — shows her exactly where the myth leaves her: driving the four oxen as they strain toward the sea. It is among the largest monuments in Copenhagen and the standard image of the goddess worldwide, and the story itself remains Denmark's foundation tale, the way Danish children learn why Zealand lies apart in the sea. Her name has even left the planet: the main-belt asteroid 1272 Gefion, discovered in 1931, gives its name to the Gefion family of asteroids. The name never became a common given name in the North, but in Denmark it needs no introduction.
lore.extendedMeditation: Gefjun is the patron of the answer that exceeds the wager. Gylfi sets the terms — four oxen, a day and a night — and keeps his word; she keeps it too, and ruins him within the terms. The myth is about measure outwitted by measure: the smallest unit of farmland, a plough-land, stretched until it holds an island and a royal house. What she gives is not only the land but the lesson the name already carries: the giver decides the scale of the gift. Every telling of her is a reminder that the terms you set will be met — by someone cleverer at keeping them.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Gefjun — already plain Latin letters, with no diacritic and no distinctive character for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved roughly ᚴᛁᚠᛁᚢᚾ (k-i-f-i-u-n: the k-rune writes g, and the single i-rune covers both the vowel e and the glide j). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: gefjun.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Gefjun is a textual goddess whose evidence is a landscape. Her attestations are literary — the Codex Regius Lokasenna, Snorri's Gylfaginning, and the Ynglinga saga of Heimskringla — and no cult site, votive deposit, or runic inscription names her; the place-name claims sometimes advanced are insecure. What the myth itself offers as evidence is the map: Zealand's headlands and the bays of Lake Mälaren, which the story explains as the two halves of a single tear. Her one fixed point on the ground is Hleiðra — Lejre, near Roskilde — where the saga seats her marriage to Skjöldr; excavations there since the 1980s have uncovered successive great-hall complexes of the Iron Age and Viking Age, confirming Lejre's real antiquity as a royal power centre, though nothing found names the goddess. The oldest datable witness to the myth is not a stone but a stanza: Bragi's ninth-century verse, quoted by both Snorri and the saga. Her most famous monument is modern: Bundgaard's Gefion Fountain in Copenhagen, unveiled 1908.
